speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Government has taken steps on multiple fronts to deal with such threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: CSA nurtures ties with the industry and raises cybersecurity awareness through public outreach programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is responsible for developing a robust cybersecurity industry and ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: CSA also seeks to strengthen cybersecurity in critical sectors, such as energy and banking, and ensure effective coordination and deployment in responding to cyber threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, educating and empowering the public to stay safe in cyberspace through public outreach programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, enhancing the Government's capacity and capability to combat cybercrime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: One key initiative was the establishment of the Police Cybercrime Command in 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Command integrates the Police's cyber-related investigations, forensics, intelligence and crime prevention capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The third priority area is stepping up close partnerships with the industry and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), as well as international engagement with foreign counterparts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The fourth area is strengthening legislation and the criminal justice framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This Bill will help ensure that our legislation remains effective in dealing with the transnational nature of cybercrime and the evolving tactics of cybercriminals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The first category involves traditional, real-world crimes that are perpetrated using a computer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Offences in this category, for example, e-commerce scams, are covered by criminal laws, such as the Penal Code.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The second category involves criminal acts that target computer systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Offences in this category are covered by the Computer Misuse and Cybersecurity Act (CMCA) which this Bill seeks to amend.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These include criminal acts like the unauthorised access of computer material and we would commonly refer to these as acts of "hacking".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This Bill will enable the Police to be more effective in dealing with this second category of cybercrime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For the first category of cybercrime, the Police will continue their current efforts, including public education and working with international counterparts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: MHA is also reviewing whether changes to other laws are required to tackle the evolving nature of how criminals are using the Internet to commit crime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This was more than double the 280 cases in 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Apart from the increase in volume, cybercrime cases have also increased in complexity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Cybercriminals use a variety of tactics and tools to carry out elaborate attacks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, the Police investigated nearly 300 cases last year, where the perpetrators hacked into victims' bank accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The criminals developed a fake banking App, with accompanying fake banking websites.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This tricked victims into keying in their personal details and login credentials, which were then stolen by these criminals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The growth of cybercrime is a global phenomenon, facilitated by technological advances and the ubiquity of the Internet and smart mobile devices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Internet of Things (IoT) devices have also been attacked.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Last October, an estimated 100,000 IoT devices were compromised and used to trigger a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack against the servers of Dyn, a company that controls much of the Internet's Domain Name System infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This disrupted major websites in the United States (US) and Europe, including Twitter, Netflix and Cable News Network (CNN).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Massive breaches of personal information have also become commonplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yahoo has suffered one of the worst data breaches, with 1.5 billion user accounts compromised over 2013 and 2014.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In April last year, the Philippines Commission on the Elections database was attacked.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Personal information belonging to 55 million voters was hacked.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Hacked personal information has been used to facilitate crimes like theft and cheating.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: On the dark web, hacked credit card information or passwords, as well as hacking tools, can be purchased easily and cheaply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The 2016 Underground Hacker Marketplace Report by Dell SecureWorks reported that stolen Visa or Mastercard details can cost as little as US$7 on the dark web.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Hacking tools, such as Remote Access Trojans, cost less than US$10.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Hackers charge a daily rate of around US$30 to US$55 for DDoS attack services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Cybercrime imposes significant costs on individual victims and the society at large.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In 2016, victims in Singapore lost about S$10 million through parcel or impersonation scams involving unauthorised access to the victims' Internet-banking accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The culprits would usually empty the victims' bank accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These financial losses are devastating to the victims because, to many of them, these monies are their life savings intended to finance the education of their children or meant for their retirement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In developing this Bill, we have taken reference from legislation in the United Kingdom (UK) and Canada.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have also consulted the cybersecurity industry to ensure that the provisions are practical and appropriately scoped.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Allow me now to take Members through the key provisions of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Broadly, the key amendments seek to address the evolving tactics of cybercriminals and the transnational nature of cybercrime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill introduces new sections 8A and 8B to address the evolving tactics of cybercriminals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Cybercriminals may deal in personal information, such as the National Registration Identity Card (NRIC) and Foreign Identification Number (FIN) numbers, credit card numbers and residential addresses, which have been illegally obtained from a computer system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Currently, our law allows us to deal with the culprit who illegally obtained personal information from a computer system, or the culprit who misused the information to commit crimes, such as impersonation and cheating.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, there may be other "middlemen" individuals who may trade in such personal information but are not directly involved in the hacking or cheating offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, criminals may run a website buying and selling hacked credit card information online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These individuals are currently not liable for an offence under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The new section 8A criminalises acts done in relation to personal information of individuals that the perpetrator knows or has reason to believe had been obtained by committing a computer crime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The act of obtaining or retaining such personal information will be an offence, as will be supplying, offering to supply, transmitting or making available that information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is not the Government's intent to criminalise legitimate cybersecurity industry practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We understand that cybersecurity professionals may deal with hacked personal information in the course of their work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For instance, they may transmit such information for the purpose of analysing a data breach or for the purpose of highlighting vulnerabilities in a system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have, therefore, introduced exceptions in section 8A.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is not an offence if the individual obtained or retained the personal information for a legitimate purpose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is also not an offence if the individual supplied, offered to supply, transmitted or made available the personal information for a legitimate purpose and they did not know or have reason to believe that the information will be or is likely to be used to commit an offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ultimately, we need to strike a balance between protecting the public interest and ensuring that legitimate practices of the cybersecurity industry can continue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It would not be difficult for bona fide cybersecurity professionals to explain why they have hacked personal information in their possession.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is also not the Police's intention to demand that every cybersecurity professional provide such explanations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Rather, in the course of investigations into a CMCA offence, the Police need to have the powers to deal with individuals who are found to have such personal information belonging to others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Fundamentally, care should be exercised when dealing with personal information, especially information that has been hacked and may be subsequently used in the commission of an offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Such items are commonly known as "hacking tools" and will include physical devices, software, passwords and access codes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The prohibited acts include obtaining or retaining the hacking tool, and making, supplying or making available the hacking tool.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To ensure that the provision does not inadvertently prohibit legitimate access by cybersecurity professionals to such tools, this is an offence only if the act is carried out with the intention of committing or facilitating the commission of a computer crime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Other jurisdictions, like the UK, have similarly made it an offence to make, supply or obtain hacking tools, where there is intent to commit or assist in committing of a computer offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Cybercriminals may conduct multiple unauthorised acts against a computer over a period of time in preparation for or as part of an actual attack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This amendment allows for multiple acts of a similar nature to be amalgamated as a single charge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This allows the attack to be appropriately described as a whole, rather than artificially segmented as a series of separate acts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Enhanced penalties may be appropriately meted out when the combined acts result in high aggregate damage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Internet is borderless, and cybercrimes are often perpetrated across geographical borders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Currently, offences in the Act apply extraterritorially only if the perpetrator or the computer, programme or data was in Singapore at the material time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This prevents enforcement action from being taken against the person who was overseas at the material time and who had targeted an overseas computer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Police will then be able to initiate investigations against cybercriminals located overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We also ensure that we establish extraterritorial jurisdiction in accordance with international norms and standards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As we forge ahead in becoming a Smart Nation, our increasing use of and reliance on technology and computers to solve our problems and better our lives bring about many benefits but also makes us more vulnerable to cybercriminals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Take, for example, the breach of MINDEF's Internet access system for servicemen and employees this year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This case was referred to by the Second Minister for Defence during Question Time today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The work appears to be targeted and not the work of a casual hacker.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If not for the Government's farsighted move last year to separate computer systems having Internet access from systems containing classified information, the impact on our country may have been worse.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While this breach may have been relatively contained, we should expect increasing attempts to breach our systems.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our laws need to be able to keep pace with such attempts and the increasing sophistication of hackers and other cybercriminals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The changes that the Bill seeks to make to CMCA, whilst not numerous, are significant in shoring up our ability to go after criminals who make use of technology to threaten our security.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, the new provisions to criminalise dealing with hacked data containing personal information for illegitimate purposes are a significant development in our fight against cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The expansion of the extraterritorial application of the CMCA offence would also allow us to address the transnational nature of cybercrimes by going after criminals who operate in the interstices of the law by disrupting our security through computers located overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have three points to make on the proposed amendments to the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the section provides that it is not an offence under that section if the person obtained or retained the personal information for a purpose other than for use or supply to be used in committing any offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The section also provides that it is not an offence under that section if the person supplied the personal information for a purpose other than to be used in committing an offence and that he did not know or have reason to believe that the information would be used to commit an offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When hacked personal data is made widely available, as in the case of Wikileaks and also in the Kbox incident in Singapore when personal data of over 300,000 customers were posted online, such data is often regarded as a treasure trove of information for certain categories of individuals, such as journalists for reporting purposes, and researchers, where such data may be useful for their research.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My reading of section 8A is that dealing with hacked personal data is only an offence when it is obtained, retained or transmitted for the purpose of supplying and/or using it in the commission of offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If my reading is correct, then it is open to journalists and researchers to deal with publicly available information obtained through computer hacking.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Perhaps, the Senior Minister of State could please clarify the Government's position to give some assurance to journalists and researchers that their obtaining and retention of such data for the purposes of their work would not cause them to fall foul of the law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, on a related point, while section 8A would go some way to deter illegitimate dealing with hacked personal data, I wonder if there may still be some unaddressed challenges in our laws.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One area is the potential for sale of personal data.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At a symposium I attended some years back, an enforcement officer spoke about the spiking of identity theft worldwide.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One unique feature of stolen personal data, unlike chattels, such as stolen paintings, is that it can be sold again and again, therein lies the economic attraction of targeting databases containing personal data.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The report also contained an account of a sales pitch given by a shady data broker who goes by the name of John Lee.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Lee claimed to have data from Groupon and other popular shopping sites in Singapore that could be purchased from him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One possible reading of the proposed section 8A is that it would not apply to Mr Lee even if Mr Lee had, in fact, obtained knowingly the personal data from a hacker, for his onward sale of data to legitimate businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because the proposed new section 8A requires the commission of an offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the sale or disclosure of personal data to others, while prohibited under the Personal Data Protection Act that attracts enforcement action by the Personal Data Commission, is not an offence per se.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If my understanding of the provision is correct, I suggest that we consider criminalising the sale of personal data obtained through unauthorised means.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without closing off this avenue, there is a danger we may be exposed to a proliferation of identity thefts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Yet, we may not be able to go after the persons responsible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, should this provision conferring extraterritorial jurisdiction be invoked, I would imagine that the Government would spare no efforts to bring the perpetrators located overseas to face justice in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With constant new challenges posed by evolving technologies, I support our efforts to guard against those who use technology to try and exploit our vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such attacks affect Government agencies as well as companies and individuals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Attacks on Government information technology (IT) systems may have national security implications.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Internationally, foreign governments or elements have been accused of hacking into political party emails or servers of other countries purportedly for political gains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An example would be the alleged hackings on the email servers during the last US presidential elections campaign.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Cyberattacks also affect businesses and individuals, causing financial losses and breach of confidential information, for example, downtime, loss of confidential business information or leaking of customer data.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In October 2016, Starhub's servers came under cyberattacks, preventing its customers from going online for two days.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The existing CMCA grants powers for law enforcement agencies to investigate and take actions against individuals or companies behind acts of cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the incidence of cyberattacks increases, as culprits of cybercrimes get bolder and smarter, we have to take appropriate and proportionate actions against such crimes and their perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, creating a new offence for obtaining items which can be used to commit an offence under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, making it an offence certain acts which are committed overseas, and targeting overseas-based computers, but which create a significant risk of serious harm in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four, amalgamating charges for offences under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I support this Bill, I have two grave concerns.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think these are fundamental issues which the prosecution should prove before another person can be charged and convicted of obtaining, retaining or making use of the information in question.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I agree that we need to enhance our efforts to tackle and prosecute cybercrimes, I still believe that we should really try to limit easing the burden of proof in this way.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This broadens the Courts' jurisdiction to offences that cause "serious harm" to Singapore, and "harm" is defined, inter alia, as "serious diminution of public confidence in the provision of any essential service or exercise of any power" in subsection (4)(b) and "a disruption of, or a serious diminution of public confidence in, the performance of any duty or function of, or the exercise of any power by the Government, an Organ of State, a Statutory Board…” and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This term "serious diminution of public confidence" seems somewhat unnecessarily broad.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does one define this term and how do we expect the Courts to decide what constitutes "serious diminution of public confidence"?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I look forward to the Senior Minister of State's clarification.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In light of the recent incidents, may I take the opportunity to ask the Government to update the House on the Government's plans for this, even though I realise it may be of a different Ministry?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, computers and websites bring us much convenience as well as elements of risk.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government's amendment of CMCA would increase cybersecurity and is a very timely action.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In May this year, the newly set up Smart Nation and Digital Government Office would strengthen cross-agency coordination and collaboration.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the area of cyber usage and security, Government agencies have already accumulated a wealth of experience.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In comparison, businesses' risk awareness and digital capability are obviously lacking.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: But in the cyberworld, enterprises can also become the target of cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I hope that the Government could transfer their wealth of experience to companies and enable the professional digital training courses offered to public servants to be promoted and made available in the business community.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We would urge companies to send their top management and core technical personnel to receive training and enable the public and private sectors to build a safety net of cybersecurity at the same time.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, businesses which make use of digital technology must strengthen their cybersecurity awareness.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In using this platform, companies' key digital data is also open to cyber risks.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I hope that in designing the platform, the Government would place the priority on cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Amendments to the Act involve sensitive information which needs protection, such as essential services like energy, water supply, banking and finance and transportation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, moving forward, businesses must be much more vigilant when they are buying or selling products, to avoid being made use of unwittingly.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, how can businesses prove that their actions are legal and aboveboard?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be a relevant agency to provide guidance to businesses and will we set up an enforcement agency to monitor the implementation of this clause?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As the amended Bill would strengthen the protection of national and individual interests, then digitalisation entails a large injection of capital, manpower and resources.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government may feel that businesses should be responsible for their own cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, these amendments could benefit a broader base of the business community and the interests of industry groups and economic entities.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: New technologies produce new conveniences, as well as new risks and new loopholes.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I support the Government's move to regularly amend related security regulations to ensure that national, individual and business interests are not compromised.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, safeguarding cybersecurity is everyone's responsibility and is a topic everyone should be concerned about.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The recent cyberattack against the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) and MINDEF that led to the leak of data belonging to almost 800 or more personnel, is a sobering reminder that Singaporeans are not immune from such attacks.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As cybercriminals become more sophisticated, so, too, must our law enforcement agencies and professionals.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is this House's solemn duty, I would say, Madam, to ensure that our laws, such as CMCA, keep apace of the developments and are refined periodically to deal with new disruptive threats.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I thus welcome the amendment Bill which seeks to finetune CMCA.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It will look at what the misuse leads to.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, it will ask whether there is significant harm or serious risk of such harm in Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is well known to international lawyers as such objective territoriality is a recognised base of jurisdiction and it has been used successfully in other pieces of legislation and is contemplated by the Securities and Futures Act and the Transboundary Haze Pollution Law as well.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would ask the Senior Minister of State respectfully though, how enforcement will be ensured.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I will add my voice to what was raised earlier by the hon Member Mr Murali Pillai, who asked whether there should be additional crank that is included into the extradition list and other forms of enforcement that the enforcement agencies or the Government would consider.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Whether there is serious harm caused in Singapore is a high threshold, Madam.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It looks at whether there was illness, injury, death, disruption of essential services in Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We can, therefore, hope to count on regulators and investigators and others in our criminal justice system who tirelessly work to uphold criminal justice in Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Having said this, Madam, I would like to ask the Ministry four questions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If so, while this may be welcomed, information and communications technology (ICT) companies and service providers should also be included in the consultation exercises, which will lead to such Bills.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Murali Pillai raised a concern that is close to my heart about whether researchers will also be restrained in some way.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond researchers, Madam, there is a further question.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will other news agencies that report on Singapore or whose Internet service providing capacities would be misused?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I am thinking about in my mind Yahoo News, Microsoft Network (MSN) news and so on.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will they also be constrained in some way?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As the cyber workspace expands, it is important to secure individuals, organisations and Singapore from being victims of cyber intrusions and cyberattacks which could hurt the very heart of Singapore's cyber connectivity and economic vibrancy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For our Smart Nation Programme to realise its objectives, a safer cybersecurity ecosystem is required, and it needs to be strengthened as new developments and tactics evolve and are exploited by cybercriminals.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the key information infrastructure operators, such as energy, finance and transport operators, be required to report on incidences of breaches or attempted breaches of cybersecurity as and when they occur rather than when directed by the Minister?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will such reporting be extended to the other business sectors, too?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Second, what is the awareness level of cybersecurity and its importance to all companies in Singapore, especially small and medium enterprises?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Do these companies see the importance of it and invest adequately in cybersecurity to protect both their individual workers' and clients' data?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be support and assistance for companies in instituting a holistic approach to protecting their cybersecurity system from cybercrime?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Third, how many organisations or companies have cyber insurances to minimise their losses or liabilities which often comes with greater awareness of cybercrimes and means to secure and tighten their cybersecurity?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, Madam, Singapore's CSA's concern on the lack of awareness of cybersecurity amongst Singaporeans is real.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: And the challenges are here to stay as our cyber transactions, cyberspace communication and cyber connectivity have increasingly become a vital part of our lives with social media use being highly pervasive.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, have we done enough and taken all possible measures to educate and increase the awareness of cybersecurity amongst students, employees, employers, social agencies as well as members of the public?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I believe there is still room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are living in a world today where many of our daily activities involve and depend on online transactions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many Singaporeans bank online, and many more do their shopping online.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This brings about greater convenience but also opens us up to new security threats.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, hackers reportedly sent out repeated phishing emails to various US institutions, and John Podesta, Chairman of Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign, allegedly clicked on one such malicious email, allowing access to over 60,000 private correspondences, some of which were subsequently leaked to the public.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fortunately, the compromised system did not contain classified or sensitive information.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This Bill will further strengthen our cybersecurity framework and I support the amendments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to seek some clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Investigating extraterritorial offences is never easy and cooperation from our foreign counterparts is crucial.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given the complexities of computer crimes and the different interpretations across jurisdictions, what is the possibility that a suspect may escape liability due to technical defects or mistakes?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With an inevitable rising cyber threat, there is a need for better qualified and highly competent cybersecurity professionals to support our cybersecurity infrastructure across both the public and private sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many companies have highlighted the shortage of such professionals locally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What about the manpower needs for the private sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any plans to build a similar technical pool of expertise for the private sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, IoT, a vast network of smart devices connecting and interacting with one another, is gaining momentum.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Personal devices and common appliances may be the weak links in our cyber defence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As in many cases, it simply takes one unknowing or unguarded individual to click on a malicious email or hyperlink and that will endanger the whole system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we enhance our public awareness, particularly for small businesses, which do not invest as much in cybersecurity?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to strengthen our cybersecurity infrastructure, enhance our legislation and, most importantly, establish a pool of cyber warriors to protect our computer systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The borderless and anonymous nature of cyberspace is an ideal hive for criminals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I support strengthening our laws on computer misuse and cybersecurity but I would like to seek clarification on several new provisions contained in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The new section 8A deals with personal information of individuals that have been obtained through hacking or other computer crimes and further using it for non-legitimate purposes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The types of personal information that is available online or on computers can vary from having one's photos on a "private" or "friends only" access on Facebook, to having more personal information, such as addresses and contact or credit card numbers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, does the provision in section 8A mean that website owners will have an added legal responsibility in watching out for unlawful information being posted as comments on their site?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The issue of online identity fraud is becoming more common and can lead to severe outcomes if not properly dealt with.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Just recently, a community leader has had his photos used not only on Facebook, but on various other online platforms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: His photo was found to have been scanned onto a digital image of a foreign passport, which was circulated online.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even without hacking or obtaining personal information through crime, cybercriminals can disrupt an individual's life by merely taking a photograph obtained online and using it for nefarious ends.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While acts of this sort are covered under provisions in the Penal Code, such as sections 415 and 416 which deal with cheating in general, or under the Protection from Harassment Act, the conditions in cyberspace could create new dimensions of committing crime that may require them to be treated separately.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the rise of such incidences in cyberspace and the convenience with which they can be committed, would the Minister consider having such incidences covered under this Bill for added deterrence?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Having new provisions in this Bill means that more manpower and expertise might be needed to investigate these cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As the field of cybersecurity is a relatively new one, do we have adequate numbers of officers trained in cybersecurity to tackle these crimes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: MINDEF recently announced that it will have a new cyber command and will rope in NSmen in cyber defence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I encourage the Home Team to take similar steps to ensure that it has enough expertise in handling an increase in cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, investigations for such cases are usually complex as it will involve dealing with the laws of other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition to that, how would distributed databases and cloud services affect investigation and enforcement?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on how this can be overcome?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What public communication plans are there to increase awareness of these issues?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How will the Ministry galvanise the support of netizens as they can play a role in combatting cybercrimes by being more vigilant when they are in cyberspace?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill provides greater assurances that our cyberspace can be a safer one.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, it would be catastrophic if the computers running our national infrastructure is compromised.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, Germany has just formed a new Cyber and Information Space Command (CIR) on 1 April 2017.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The new command will be on par with the army, navy and air force.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Besides disrupting our lives, what is deeply worrying is that a successful large-scale cyberattack would result in the loss of trust and faith in Singapore's systems, from businesses and investors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I had asked about the issue of how the Police are tackling cybercrimes previously and am glad that the Police have set up a Cybercrime Command within the Criminal Investigation Department in 2015.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In this latest set of amendments, the toughening of legal clout against the act of dealing and trading in personal information, the buying and selling of hacking tools, and offences that are committed abroad which may cause serious harm to Singapore, will certainly build on what has already been done to strengthen Singapore's cybersecurity and resilience.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, technology is constantly evolving and I am certain new situations will arise which may require further strengthening of our laws in future.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For instance, is it an offence to set up a fake Facebook account?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But several of my Parliamentary colleagues and I have had fake Facebook accounts set up in our names, and once the perpetrators successfully befriend our friends, they proceed to ask for donations through private messages.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Fortunately, no money was transacted as my friends were rightly suspicious, but in such situations should the Police be given powers to investigate fake Facebook accounts?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Being strong in cybersecurity also presents an economic opportunity which Singapore can leverage on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Israel is a world leader in cybersecurity solutions and its cybersecurity exports totaled $6 billion in 2014.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Interestingly, it was a top-down initiative which started with a directive by Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With Singapore's interest, investment and emphasis on the digital economy, we are well-placed to become the cybersecurity equivalent of Israel in Asia if we can get our act together.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Although it is important to toughen the laws to deter the hackers and mete out harsher penalties to them, prevention is even more critical.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I believe that the Singapore Cybercrime Command and the soon-to-be established DCO under MINDEF will help us map out national and defence cybersecurity strategies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, the key is whether we have enough computer specialists, in particular, cybersecurity professionals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In this respect, I hope that the Government can adopt a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: First, we should train more cyber specialists, with a focus on cybersecurity professionals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We all know that most of our top performing students choose medicine or law, because lawyers and doctors tend to earn big money.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We need to encourage some of these top students to study computer science instead.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Offering attractive scholarships is one way, formulating an IT professional development roadmap is equally important to prevent a brain drain in the IT sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: To attract more top students to choose scholarships in computer science and better tap on computer specialists who are serving National Service, I suggest that MINDEF allow Singaporeans serving full-time National Service who have been awarded scholarships to study IT to be disrupted from NS to complete their tertiary education first before returning to serve in DCO.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is similar to allowing medical students to return to serve in the army after they have obtained their medical degrees.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the same vein, returning computer specialists can help guard against computer viruses and cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is "killing two birds with one stone".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, we also need to boost the general knowledge of IT and cybersecurity at the base level.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, it is not clear from the newspaper report which group of civil servants will be trained by NUS.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our laws must keep up with the fast-evolving nature of cyber activities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a timely Bill which will empower the Ministry to deal with the increasing number of cybercrimes, including the unauthorised use of personal information and the trade and tools to facilitate such illegal usage.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that for the "SMEs Go Digital" programme which was announced at this year's Budget, areas, such as cybersecurity and data protection, are included.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge the Government to also use this programme as a one-stop platform for SMEs to keep their companies abreast of new developments in cyber defences and to share their experiences in countering cyberattacks, the protection of digital properties and recovery processes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such mutual support and even collaborations will be helpful for the prevention of future attacks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ideally, all offences should be reported so that the Ministry will have a better overview of criminal activities in this landscape, which will inform current and future policies to protect our systems as a whole.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry also share the progress of its various cyber awareness programmes targeting different segments of our community, from our students to the elderly?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does the Ministry gauge the effectiveness of these programmes in reducing the number of cybercrime victims?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our legislative framework cannot be enforced without these talents to protect our systems and track down the perpetrators of cyber offences.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How are we going to overcome the problem of these IT specialist shortages, particularly in the middle and senior ranks?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We live in an increasingly connected world, but the Internet has also created a multitude of opportunities for criminals to thrive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Quite a few Members of this House have recently had their Facebook identities stolen and used to send phishing messages.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure that came as a rude shock, but at least my colleagues had the capacity to deal with the matter quickly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I fear, however, that many Singaporeans do not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, it recognises that sophisticated software, in the hands of wrong persons, can be as dangerous as giving them physical weapons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, it criminalises acts of cybersecurity that originate physically outside our borders but passed through or target computers within.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, it criminalises the use of personal data that have been obtained through hacks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All three changes are necessary steps to build a society that is more resilient to cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this could be a needed move in light of the increased cyberattacks and misuse of information, I am concerned with the drafting of section 8A(6) that fellow Member Mr Dennis Tan had raised previously.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By way of background, section 8A(1) penalises people who use personal information that arises from the contravention of certain sections of the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, could a perpetrator truly and accurately know that one of the relevant sections was contravened at the time of the offence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the burden of proof required under this section?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I am concerned that there is a growing digital divide that is leaving our Pioneer Generation behind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have many elderly residents who do not know how to use a computer properly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I am concerned that our elderly are vulnerable to cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Anecdotes of the elderly falling victim to scams are plenty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, can there be a collaboration with the Pioneer Generation Office with regard to IT resilience for our Pioneer Generation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, may I also suggest coordinated grassroots campaigns in relation to cybersecurity be launched?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under these campaigns, grassroots leaders (GRLs) can reach out to the elderly on topics, such as how to spot phishing emails or messages and how to protect themselves against cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that as we continue to push towards being a smart and connected nation, we should also not leave behind anyone and ensure that all of us are protected against cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, cyberspace presents new opportunities for criminals to operate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hacking tools are readily available and criminals can misuse these tools to carry out attacks on computer systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many criminals commit computer offences to illegally obtain personal information which can then be used, in turn, to carry out offences like theft and fraud.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Cybercriminals are emboldened by the fact that computer offences can be carried out from overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will use two previous examples of cybercrime cases to illustrate the need for this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members may recall the case of hacker James Raj.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: James Raj, who adopted the pseudonym "The Messiah", was convicted of numerous charges under the Act for committing a series of hacks in 2013.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He was responsible for hacking the server of Fuji Xerox, the Straits Times' blog, as well as the websites of certain Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Various hacking tools were also found on the system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Three of the Chinese nationals were later found to have committed criminal offences while in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: James Sim's actions enabled criminals to breach Singapore's immigration and border protection system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These two cases show that the amendments in this Bill are necessary to deal with the unique law enforcement challenges posed by cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The amendments to the Act will enable the Police to effectively deal with the evolving tactics of cybercriminals and the transnational nature of cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Several Members spoke about the new sections 8A and 8B of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to strike a balance between protecting the public interest and ensuring that legitimate cybersecurity industry practices can continue because they contribute to the overall atmosphere of cybersecurity in Singapore and elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have, therefore, introduced exceptions in these provisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These were drafted in consultation with stakeholders from the cybersecurity industry, telecommunications companies (telcos) and Internet Service Providers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With these exceptions, legitimate practices will not be criminalised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is a broad definition and can include addresses, dates of birth and credit card numbers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These information types are sold online often for criminal gain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Personal photographs may, depending on the circumstances, be considered personal information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Depending on the facts of the case on how the photographs are obtained and used, there may be other Penal Code offences, such as cheating by personation or harassment under the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Section 8A will only apply if the personal information in question was obtained through a computer crime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng referred to the recent cases of Members of this House having been impersonated via fake Facebook accounts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hacking an existing Facebook account is already an offence under CMCA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Creating a fake Facebook account is not a CMCA offence in itself.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But depending on the facts of the case, for instance, if cheating is involved, other Penal Code offences, such as cheating by personation, may have been committed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether a journalist or a researcher dealing with hacked personal information in the course of their work would have committed an offence under the new section 8A.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is nothing wrong with the journalist reporting on the hacking incident or the researcher who works with the hacked personal information for research purposes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it is doubtful if they would ever need to disclose the hacked personal information itself, as part of the report or research findings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, there is no need for them to publish details, such as hacked credit card numbers, as part of the report on the hacking incident or the research findings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Depending on the circumstances, indiscriminately making available hacked personal information may amount to an offence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Care should always be exercised where hacked personal information is transmitted, even if for a legitimate purpose.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This could be done by ensuring that the information is only transmitted to trusted persons who have a legitimate reason to receive the information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where possible, the personal information should be redacted or anonymised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked if website owners have an added responsibility to watch out for unlawful information posted on their sites.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Website owners who are aware of hacked personal information hosted on their servers are encouraged to report this to the authorities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is no different for anyone who comes across hacked personal information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Dennis Tan spoke about the prosecution not having to prove the particulars of the computer offence through which the personal information was obtained, that is, no need to prove the predicate offence when prosecuting the case of a person under section 8A.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The prosecution, first, has to prove that the person involved knew or had reason to believe that the personal information was obtained by an act of hacking, in contravention of CMCA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There will be cases where it will be clear from the circumstances that the information in question could only have been obtained by hacking.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, if there is evidence to show that credit card numbers were purchased from a website that trades in hacked credit card information, or if there is an entire file of bank account passwords that the person downloaded from such a site.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it can be practically difficult for the prosecution to also prove the particulars of the actual hacking offence for each of the pieces of information found on the site containing information that had been obtained through hacking.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the earlier example where the credit card numbers were purchased from an illegal website, the identity of the hacker and the exact time when the hack took place may not be known, or easily verifiable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Murali Pillai made several points about data protection, including how the provisions in CMCA and the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) would apply.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: PDPA establishes various rules governing the collection, use and disclosure of personal data by organisations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It recognises both the needs of organisations to collect, use and disclose personal data for legitimate and reasonable purposes and the rights of individuals to have their personal data adequately protected from intentional misuse and unauthorised disclosure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Section 8A criminalises acts done in relation to personal information of individuals that the perpetrator knows or has reason to believe has been obtained through a computer crime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA's intent is to prevent the misuse of such hacked personal information for criminal purposes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, in a scenario where a report was received regarding the online posting of hacked personal information belonging, say, to customers of a company, the Police would investigate whether a criminal offence under section 8A had been committed by the person who posted the information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) would look into whether the company had made reasonable security arrangements to prevent the unauthorised access of this personal information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police and the Commission will work closely together in dealing with such cases and ensure that there is no overlap in investigation responsibilities, while protecting the public's interest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But depending on the circumstances, this may be covered under other laws.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will consider the Member's suggestion in the review of these other pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Several Members highlighted the need for the private sector to level up cybersecurity by strengthening cybersecurity awareness among businesses, like growing cybersecurity expertise in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are both focus areas in Singapore's cybersecurity strategy and are led by CSA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Cybersecurity is a collective responsibility and everyone, whether individuals or businesses, has a role to play in making cyberspace a safer place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To promote cybersecurity awareness, the Government has been running the Cybersecurity Awareness Campaign since 2011.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Cybersecurity Awareness Alliance, started in 2008, brings together Government agencies, private enterprises and professional associations to promote the adoption of essential cybersecurity practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Singapore Computer Emergency Response Team (SingCERT) under CSA provides advisories to help businesses pre-empt and prevent cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Businesses are also encouraged to read cybersecurity tips and resources on CSA's GoSafeOnline website.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Thanaletchimi spoke about keeping SMEs informed of the latest developments in cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Tech Hub will provide technical advice to SMEs with more advanced digital needs, such as cybersecurity and data analytics.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Hub will help to connect SMEs to ICT vendors and consultants, as well as conduct workshops and seminars to help SMEs build their digital capabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On their part, businesses must also recognise and treat cyber risks as important business risks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government is also collaborating with industry to grow the cybersecurity workforce for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, under the Cyber Security Associates and Technologists (CSAT) programme, CSA and IMDA work with the industry and IHLs to attract new graduates and convert existing professionals from related fields.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our universities and polytechnics are also offering cybersecurity programmes for those keen to pursue cybersecurity education.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These efforts will go a long way towards creating a vibrant cybersecurity ecosystem for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan and Mr Dennis Tan asked if there would be other cybersecurity legislation and what its shape would be like.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will also convey various Members' suggestions and feedback to CSA and MCI for their consideration as they work on the Cybersecurity Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The perpetrators of cyber incidents, which CSA would manage, might have committed an offence under CMCA in the process of carrying out the attack.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Thomas Chua, Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Dennis Tan spoke about widening the extraterritorial jurisdiction of the Bill beyond acts that result in serious harm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As mentioned, offences in CMCA currently have extraterritorial effect if the perpetrator or the computer, programme or data was in Singapore at the material time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, the act of hacking a computer which was located in Singapore would already be covered by the Act, even if the perpetrator were located overseas at the material time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked how cloud services and distributed databases affect enforcement and investigation of cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, an increasing amount of data that is hosted on the cloud may actually be physically stored in servers located overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is a challenge faced by law enforcement agencies worldwide.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where necessary, the Police will work with overseas counterparts to investigate such cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The amendment in clause 4 will allow such cases to be charged and prosecuted before our Courts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, we have scoped the definition of "serious harm in Singapore" carefully, so that the cases we investigate and prosecute are those that have a significant impact in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These may include cases where there is illness, injury or death caused to individuals in Singapore; a disruption of essential services, such as services directly related to public transportation, banking and finance and public utilities; a disruption of the performance of any duty or function of the Government; and where there is damage to the national security, defence or foreign relations of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked that we also include as serious harm any act that damages the economy of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The definition of essential services already takes into consideration the critical sectors that will affect the economy, should they be attacked.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Dennis Tan wanted to know how the amended section 11 subsection 4 paragraph (c), in the definition of "serious harm in Singapore", will be operationalised in respect of the sub-clause on "serious diminution of public confidence" in Government services or the disruption of Government functions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: What constitutes a "serious diminution of public confidence" would certainly depend on the facts of the case, but there are examples in the Bill of acts that seriously diminish or create a significant risk of seriously diminishing public confidence in the performance of any duty or function of or the exercise of the power by the Government, an Organ of State or a Statutory Board.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These examples include providing to the public access to confidential documents belonging to a Ministry of the Government, as well as publication to the public of the access codes for a computer belonging to a Statutory Board.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Thomas Chua asked for similar protection for essential services to be extended to NTP.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I hope that is the correct interpretation or translation of what the Member said in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NTP can be considered as supporting an "essential service" as currently defined in CMCA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is also a function provided by the Government.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, depending on the actual situation, a disruption to this could be considered within the scope of "serious harm" in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Desmond Choo spoke about the challenges of investigating cybercrimes committed overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is another reason why the provisions have to be scoped, so as to ensure that Police resources are not over-committed to pursue crimes that have limited or no impact on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the cases that are investigated, the Police will work closely with overseas counterparts to provide and share evidence of such cases, with a view to prosecuting the criminals in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan both asked if we will make CMCA offences extraditable under the Extradition Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Desmond Choo and Ms Joan Pereira gave various suggestions on how to deal with cybercrime, and I thank them for that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Last year, MHA launched NCAP, which I referred to in my opening statement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NCAP sets out the Government's key principles and priorities in combating cybercrime, and amending CMCA is one of the key initiatives of NCAP.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under NCAP, we have also enhanced public education and outreach efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Mr Desmond Choo said, the public can play a role in combating cybercrimes by being more vigilant in cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng and Ms Joan Pereira spoke about outreach efforts for vulnerable groups, such as young students and the elderly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police work closely with schools and organisations, such as the Media Literacy Council, to raise awareness of cybercrimes among these vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police have also been using existing senior citizen engagement platforms, such as IMDA's Silver IT Fest, to raise the cybercrime awareness of senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Joan Pereira also asked how we would encourage companies to step forward and report cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police also regularly reach out to smaller businesses as well to share information on cybercrimes and cybercrime prevention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked how we would educate the general public on the provisions of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our public cybercrime outreach programmes are principally focused on how to prevent members of the public from falling victim to cybercrimes, but most members of the public would not use hacking tools or transmit hacked personal information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we agree that there is a need to reach out to the cybersecurity industry as well as to students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA has worked with organisations, such as the Singapore Infocomm Technology Federation (SiTF), to publicise information about the new provisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to work with CSA on outreach efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also stepped up enforcement actions against cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked what steps the Home Team will be taking to ensure that it has sufficient expertise to handle the increase in cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have been building up new capabilities in the fight against cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I had spoken earlier about the role of the Police Cybercrime Command in coordinating an effective response to cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also set up Cybercrime Response Teams in every Police Land Divisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The teams augment the manpower available to respond to cybercrime reports by assisting investigation officers in responding to cybercrime reports through collecting and processing digital evidence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also been working closely with industry and IHLs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, Temasek Polytechnic and MHA are developing a TALENT Lab, which will be used to train students from IHLs in cybercrime investigations and forensic skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Lab will be officially opened later this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also continued to strengthen our international partnerships.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Last year, MHA, the Attorney-General's Chambers and CSA organised the first Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Cybercrime Prosecutors' Roundtable Meeting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This event brought together ASEAN cybercrime prosecutors to share their experiences in addressing cybercrime cases and build networks among the prosecutors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These efforts to fight cybercrime have started to show encouraging results.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, these cases, along with scams, like Internet love scams and officials impersonation scams, still remain a significant crime concern.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to monitor the cybercrime situation and calibrate our outreach programme and enforcement efforts accordingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA will continue its efforts under NCAP, in partnership with industry, IHLs, the public and law enforcement agencies, so that we can, collectively, create a safe and secure online environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The threats have so far been under control, but it lurks in many dark corners of cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We, therefore, need to put in place a robust legislative framework with safeguards, but also with the necessary enforcement levers as part of a comprehensive cybercrime and cybersecurity strategy, to ensure that our computers, systems and data are better protected.
